doc.title: Herbie Hancock interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 18, 1995

title: Don Goldberg and discovering George Shearing
summary: A classmate improvising in a trio fascinated him; he found he already owned Shearing records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And I said I want to be like that. So I started hanging out with them. And you hang out with them, they’re listening to jazz. So that was one of the things. That was one of the things. There was another very important thing too. There was a pianist named Don Goldberg who performed at the variety show that my school used to give every semester. And he had a jazz trio. And he was my age, he was in my class, and I heard him improvising and I was shocked first of all. It sounded, I didn’t know what he was doing. Because I always used to turn jazz off whenever it was on the radio, because I didn’t understand it and I didn’t want to know anything about it, I didn’t care about it, I didn’t like it. But when I saw this guy improvising and it sounded organized to me. I didn’t know what he was doing but it sounded like he knew what he was doing. Then I became fascinated. ‘Cause he was doing it on my instrument and he was my age. I thought you had to be much older to play jazz you know, like nineteen or something. But he was doing it. And so I started hanging out with this guy and asking him what is he listening to, how does he learn that, how do you do these things. And so at the time, his favorite pianist and the person he tried to emulate was George Shearing. So I remember going home telling my mother, “Mama, you’ve got to get me some George Shearing records.” And she said, “Son, you have some George Shearing records.” I said, “No mama, you

don’t understand. I want to get some George Shearing records. I got to find out how to do this improvising you know.” She said, “Herbie, remember those records I bought for you about two years ago and you got angry with me because you didn’t know who it was and there were some other records you wanted and you had a tantrum about seeing these records for Christmas?” I said, “Yeah.” She said, “That was George Shearing. And you’ve got those records in your cabinet.” So I went in the cabinet and sure enough, they were there. My mother had no idea that that was going to be the first jazz artist I would ask about. It just was—
